requirements: The core contributions of the paper 'KIVI: A Tuning-Free Asymmetric 2bit Quantization for KV Cache' have been reproduced, including the asymmetric per-channel key / per-token value 2-bit quantization scheme, the streaming grouped+residual data structure, and the accuracy and throughput results on LM-Eval, LongBench, and NIAH benchmarks.

The Needle-in-a-Haystack (NIAH) passkey retrieval evaluation from Appendix B / Figure 4 is prepared: Paul Graham essays as background filler, the Mohtashami & Jaggi prompt template with a 7-digit passkey, and a depth×length sweep.

Code has been implemented that downloads or vendors the Paul Graham essays corpus from https://paulgraham.com/articles.html (footnote 2) and concatenates them into a background text long enough to reach at least the 20K-word / ~30K-token upper end of the sweep shown in Figure 4.
The passkey used in each NIAH prompt is a freshly sampled uniformly-random 7-digit integer (per Appendix B "but using 7-digit passkey").

The NIAH prompt template matches Appendix B verbatim: the fixed preamble "There is an important info hidden inside a lot of irrelevant text...", the Paul Graham prefix filler, the two-sentence needle "The pass key is <7-DIGIT PASS KEY>. Remember it. <7-DIGIT PASS KEY> is the pass key.", a suffix filler, and the terminal question "What is the pass key? The pass key is".

The needle is inserted at a configurable depth d ∈ [0.0, 1.0] such that the prefix filler occupies the first d·L characters/words of the filler budget and the suffix filler occupies the remainder, so depth 0.0 places the needle at the start and 1.0 at the end.

The NIAH sweep enumerates the same depth×length grid shown in Figure 4: 10 depth positions {0.0, 0.11, 0.22, 0.33, 0.44, 0.56, 0.67, 0.78, 0.89, 1.0} × 10 word-count buckets {0.5K, 2K, 4K, 7K, 9K, 11K, 13K, 16K, 18K, 20K}.

The x-axis label of each Figure-4 heatmap is measured in word count (not tokens) and the final total token length is annotated in the upper-right corner ("20K words   27K tokens", etc.), matching Figure 4's caption "we count the number of words instead of tokens to better account for the tokenizer difference".

The NIAH scorer extracts the model's continuation after "The pass key is" and returns 1.0 iff it contains the exact 7-digit passkey (0.0 otherwise); scores are aggregated per (depth, length) cell and rendered as the 0-1 colored heatmap shown in Figure 4.

The empirical analysis of KV cache element distribution from Section 3.1, Section 3.2, Figure 2 and Table 2 is reproduced, and the OB1/OB2/OB3 observations that motivate KIVI's asymmetric quantization scheme are derived from measured numbers rather than restated from the paper.

An analysis harness collects per-layer/per-head KV cache tensors from Llama-2-13B (multi-head attention) and Falcon-7B (multi-query attention) that the distribution study, Figure 2 visualization, and Table 2 error tables all consume.

Code has been implemented that registers forward hooks (or patches the attention module) to capture the pre-quantization key and value cache tensors for every transformer layer and every head of a HuggingFace Llama-2-13B model during a forward pass.

Code has been implemented that captures the pre-quantization key and value cache tensors for every layer of a HuggingFace Falcon-7B model, correctly handling that Falcon-7B uses multi-query attention with a single KV head shared across query heads.

Code has been implemented that drives the analysis models with a fixed calibration prompt / sequence of at least the number of tokens shown along the token axis of Figure 2 (~200 tokens) so that captured KV tensors have shape (num_tokens, num_channels) per head/layer.

The captured KV cache tensor for a given (model, layer, head) is a 2D float tensor whose leading dimension is the token count and trailing dimension equals the model's per-head channel dimension (128 for Llama-2-13B, 64 for Falcon-7B).

The Figure 2 visualization of KV cache absolute-value distributions is reproduced for Llama-2-13B and Falcon-7B, showing the per-channel outlier structure in the key cache and the absence of an outlier pattern in the value cache.
Code has been implemented that renders a 3D bar (or surface) plot of the absolute value of a KV cache tensor as a function of (token index, channel index), matching the style used in Figure 2.
The visualization pipeline produces the four Llama-2-13B panels of Figure 2: layer 16 head 0 key cache, layer 16 head 0 value cache, layer 31 head 0 key cache, and layer 31 head 0 value cache.
The visualization pipeline produces the four Falcon-7B panels of Figure 2: layer 16 head 0 key cache, layer 16 head 0 value cache, layer 20 head 0 key cache, and layer 20 head 0 value cache.

For every Llama-2-13B / Falcon-7B key-cache panel, a small set of channels have magnitudes that dominate the other channels across the token axis (per-channel outlier structure): the ratio of max-channel-mean-|value| to median-channel-mean-|value| exceeds 5x.

For every Llama-2-13B / Falcon-7B value-cache panel, no small subset of channels dominates: the ratio of max-channel-mean-|value| to median-channel-mean-|value| is small (well below the corresponding ratio measured on the key cache from the same layer/head).
Peak absolute value in the reproduced Llama-2-13B key-cache plots (layer 16 and layer 31, head 0) is within tolerance of the ~10-12.5 peaks shown in Figure 2 for those panels.
Peak absolute value in the reproduced Falcon-7B key-cache plots (layer 16 and layer 20, head 0) is within tolerance of the ~8-10 peaks shown in Figure 2 for those panels.

An error-analysis harness implements the reconstruction, attention-score, attention-sparsity, and attention-output-error metrics used to populate Table 2, running under fake per-token and per-channel 2-bit quantization on Llama-2-13B.

Code has been implemented that fake-quantizes-then-dequantizes a captured KV cache tensor with 2-bit precision using group size 32 in either the per-token or per-channel direction, matching the Section 3.1 fake-quant definition.
Code has been implemented that computes the relative Frobenius reconstruction error ||X - X'||_F / ||X||_F for a KV cache tensor and its fake-quantized counterpart.

Code has been implemented that computes the relative attention-score error ||A - A'||_F / ||A||_F where A = Softmax(t_Q X_K^T) is the full-precision attention score row and A' uses the quantize/dequantized key cache.

Code has been implemented that computes the attention-output relative error Delta = ||A X_V - A X_V'||_F / ||A X_V||_F using the full-precision attention scores and both full-precision and fake-quantized value caches.

Code has been implemented that computes an attention-sparsity metric measuring what fraction of the attention-score mass lies in a small set of tokens (e.g. the smallest k contributing >=99% of the row sum) over Llama-2-13B attention rows.

The error harness averages each of the reconstruction, attention-score, and Delta metrics over all layers and all heads of Llama-2-13B (producing a single scalar per configuration, matching the 'Avg.' rows in Table 2).
The nine numerical entries of Table 2 for Llama-2-13B under 2-bit per-token vs per-channel quantization are reproduced within tolerance.
Average key-cache relative reconstruction error under per-token 2-bit quantization on Llama-2-13B is within tolerance of the reported 13.67.
Average key-cache relative reconstruction error under per-channel 2-bit quantization on Llama-2-13B is within tolerance of the reported 4.55.

Average relative attention-score error using per-token-quantized keys on Llama-2-13B is within tolerance of the reported 47.00, and is roughly 5x larger than the per-channel counterpart (consistent with Section 3.2).
Average relative attention-score error using per-channel-quantized keys on Llama-2-13B is within tolerance of the reported 9.60.
Measured Llama-2-13B attention sparsity is within tolerance of the reported 84.3%.
Average value-cache relative reconstruction error under per-token 2-bit quantization on Llama-2-13B is within tolerance of the reported 4.57.
Average value-cache relative reconstruction error under per-channel 2-bit quantization on Llama-2-13B is within tolerance of the reported 3.73.
Average attention-output error Delta on Llama-2-13B with per-token-quantized value cache is within tolerance of the reported 3.55.

Average attention-output error Delta on Llama-2-13B with per-channel-quantized value cache is within tolerance of the reported 49.89, i.e. more than an order of magnitude larger than the per-token value-cache Delta.

Observations OB1, OB2 and OB3 from Section 3.1, together with the explanatory analyses in Section 3.2, are derived from the reproduced numbers rather than restated verbatim, and are recorded in a written analysis artifact next to the numerical tables.

The analysis report explicitly derives OB1 by pointing to the reproduced Llama-2-13B numbers: 4-bit per-token quantization of both K and V cache maintains full-precision accuracy on CoQA and TruthfulQA, while 2-bit per-token quantization causes a large drop.

The analysis report explicitly derives OB2 by pointing to reproduced numbers showing that per-channel value-cache quantization causes a severe accuracy collapse (both (K-C, V-C) and (K-T, V-C) rows near zero) regardless of how the key cache is quantized.

The analysis report explicitly derives OB3 by pointing to reproduced numbers showing that at 2 bits the (K per-channel, V per-token) configuration attains the highest CoQA and TruthfulQA scores among all four 2-bit configurations for Llama-2-13B.

The analysis report links Figure 2's per-channel outlier structure in the key cache to the Table 2 measurements (K per-channel error 4.55 vs per-token 13.67; attention-score error 9.60 vs 47.00) as evidence for per-channel key-cache quantization.

The analysis report links the Table 2 value-cache measurements (Delta = 3.55 per-token vs 49.89 per-channel, together with the 84.3% attention sparsity) to the Equation (2) argument that per-token value-cache quantization confines error to individual tokens and is preferred despite the absence of channel-wise outliers.
The asymmetric B-bit round-to-nearest quantize / dequantize primitives with per-token and per-channel group-wise scaling factors and zero-points are implemented as defined in Section 3.1.

The B-bit round-to-nearest quantize and dequantize functions from Section 3.1 (with per-group zero-point z_X = min X and scaling factor s_X = (max X - min X)/(2^B - 1)) are implemented as standalone primitives.

Code has been implemented that provides a quantize function taking a floating-point tensor X, a bit-width B, and a group axis (token or channel) and returning a B-bit unsigned integer code tensor together with per-group zero-points and per-group scaling factors.

Code has been implemented that provides a dequantize function taking integer codes, zero-points, and scaling factors and returning the reconstructed floating-point tensor X' = round((X-z_X)/s_X) * s_X + z_X of the original shape.
The zero-point for each group is computed as the minimum value of the tensor over that group, matching z_X = min X in Section 3.1.
The scaling factor for each group is computed as s_X = (max X - min X) / (2^B - 1), matching the definition in Section 3.1.
The rounding operation ⌊·⌉ used inside quantize is round-to-nearest (as opposed to floor/ceil/truncation), matching the round-to-nearest quantization defined in Section 3.1.
The integer codes emitted by quantize are clamped to the range [0, 2^B - 1] so that no code exceeds the B-bit representable range for any B (in particular B=2 and B=4).
Per-token and per-channel group-wise quantization axes and the configurable group size G / bit-width B are supported as illustrated in Figure 1.

Code has been implemented for per-token quantization that groups elements along the channel dimension of X (shape l_prompt x d) so each group is a contiguous block of G channels within a single token, as shown in Figure 1 (left).

Code has been implemented for per-channel quantization that groups elements along the token dimension of X so each group is a contiguous block of G tokens within a single channel, as shown in Figure 1 (right).
The group size G is a configurable parameter of the quantization primitives (with 32 as the default matching Section 4.1) and controls the number of elements per group along the grouped axis.
The bit-width B is a configurable parameter of the quantization primitives and at minimum both B=2 and B=4 (as used by KIVI-2 and KIVI-4) are supported end-to-end through quantize and dequantize.
Structural helpers for the fake quantization used in Section 3.1's preliminary study exist so that any of the four (K-T/K-C) x (V-T/V-C) configurations can be simulated.

Code has been implemented for a fake_quantize wrapper that returns dequantize(quantize(X)) as a single call, used in the attention layer to simulate quantization without changing dtype at the interface level (matching the fake quantization setting described in Section 3.1).

Code has been implemented that dispatches per-token vs per-channel quantization by an axis argument so that key and value caches can independently be configured to any of the four combinations {K-T, K-C} x {V-T, V-C} required by Table 1.

Code has been implemented that zero-pads the token dimension so it is divisible by G before performing per-channel group-wise quantization, matching the padding method described in Section 3.1 for the fake-quantization comparison.
Deterministic behavioral properties of the quantize/dequantize primitives are verified so that shapes, code ranges, and reconstruction bounds match the definitions.
For per-token quantization on an input of shape (T, D) with D divisible by G, quantize returns integer codes of shape (T, D), zero-points of shape (T, D/G), and scaling factors of shape (T, D/G).
For per-channel quantization on an input of shape (T, D) with T divisible by G, quantize returns integer codes of shape (T, D), zero-points of shape (T/G, D), and scaling factors of shape (T/G, D).
For every group, the maximum absolute reconstruction error |X - dequantize(quantize(X))| does not exceed the group's scaling factor s_X (i.e., the rounding bound implied by (max-min)/(2^B - 1)).

Re-quantizing the dequantized tensor is idempotent — the second call to quantize on dequantize(quantize(X)) produces the same integer codes as the first call — confirming the round-to-nearest primitive is deterministic.
On a constant tensor (all elements equal) the quantizer produces s_X = 0 (or a numerically safe substitute) without producing NaN/Inf and dequantize reconstructs the original constant exactly.

The KIVI prefill and decoding algorithm from Section 3.3 / Algorithm 1 is implemented, including grouped vs residual key/value splits, KeyQuant procedure, per-token value quantization, decoding-time flushes when residual buffer reaches R, and the tiled mixed-precision attention computation.
The KIVI KV cache data structure separately maintains a quantized grouped part and a full-precision residual part for both keys and values with configurable group size G and residual length R.

Code has been implemented that stores the KV cache for each layer as the four-tuple (Q(X_Kg), X_Kr, Q(X_Vg), X_Vr), where Q(X_Kg) and Q(X_Vg) are quantized tensors and X_Kr, X_Vr are full-precision residual buffers.
Code has been implemented that exposes group size G and residual length R as configuration hyperparameters with defaults G=32 and R=128 as used in the paper.
Code enforces (or documents and validates) that the residual length R is divisible by the group size G, as required by Section 3.3.
Code initializes the residual buffers X_Kr and X_Vr as empty full-precision tensors and the grouped quantized tensors as empty at the start of each sequence.

The Prefill procedure from Algorithm 1 is implemented, computing K/V for the prompt, splitting into grouped and residual parts, quantizing each, and returning full-precision K/V for the current layer's attention.
Code computes X_K = X W_K and X_V = X W_V for the prompt of length l_prompt during the prefill phase before any splitting or quantization.
Code splits the value cache during prefill as X_Vg = X_V[:l_prompt - R] and X_Vr = X_V[l_prompt - R:], preserving the last R value tokens in full precision.
Code applies per-token group-wise quantization to X_Vg with numGroup = d // G along the channel-partitioned direction (dim=token) as specified in Algorithm 1.
Code invokes KeyQuant(X_K) during prefill to produce Q(X_Kg) and X_Kr, and stores them together with Q(X_Vg) and X_Vr in the KV cache slot.

Code returns the exact full-precision (X_K, X_V) tensors from the prefill procedure so that the current layer's attention output is computed without quantization error, while only the compressed cache is retained for future decoding steps.

When prompt length l_prompt < R, the prefill procedure gracefully places all tokens into X_Vr (and X_Kr) instead of producing negative-length slices, matching the intended semantics of the sliding window.
The KeyQuant sub-procedure that splits X_K by residue and applies per-channel group-wise quantization to the grouped part is implemented as specified in Algorithm 1.

On flush, code concatenates the newly quantized Q(X_Kr) with the existing Q(X_Kg) along the token dimension so that the grouped key cache monotonically grows in blocks of R tokens.

On value flush, code concatenates Q(X_Vr') with the existing Q(X_Vg) along the token dimension.

Code concatenates the grouped and residual raw logits along the token dimension to form the full attention pre-softmax vector A, matching the Concat in Algorithm 1.
Code applies a single softmax over the concatenated logits (grouped + residual) rather than softmaxing the two parts independently, preserving joint normalization across all cached tokens.
Code splits the softmax output into A_g = Softmax(A)[:-R] and A_r = Softmax(A)[-R:] according to the size of the residual buffer.

The fused dequantization + mixed-precision matmul (Q_MatMul) CUDA kernel and the Triton group-wise quantization kernel described in Section 3.3 are implemented and integrated into the attention path.

A CUDA Q_MatMul kernel is implemented that fuses dequantization of the quantized grouped key cache with the query × K^T matrix multiplication at the tiling level, avoiding materialization of a full FP16 dequantized K.
Kernel source and build wiring exist.

Code has been implemented containing at least one CUDA source file (e.g. `.cu`) that defines a kernel implementing the fused dequantization + mixed-precision matmul (Q_MatMul) shown in Figure 3 for KIVI.

Code has been implemented that exposes the CUDA Q_MatMul kernel to Python via a PyTorch C++/CUDA extension (pybind or `torch.utils.cpp_extension.load`) with a documented callable signature accepting the query tensor, packed low-bit key tensor, per-group scales, and per-group zero-points.

Code has been implemented such that the CUDA extension for Q_MatMul builds successfully on an NVIDIA GPU environment (matching the paper's A100 target) and can be imported from Python without runtime linker/JIT errors.
The Q_MatMul kernel implements the fused mixed-precision behavior described in Section 3.3.

The Q_MatMul kernel accepts a 2-bit packed representation of the grouped key cache (e.g. INT8 buffers packing four 2-bit codes per byte) together with its per-group scale and zero-point, and produces the FP16/BF16 attention-logit output for `q @ dequant(K_g)^T`.
The Q_MatMul kernel additionally supports a 4-bit packed key representation (KIVI-4 path) using the same fused-dequant + matmul flow.

The kernel performs dequantization inside the matmul tile loop (registers/shared memory) and never writes a full FP16 dequantized K back to global memory before the matmul, matching the "fuses the dequantization with matrix multiplication at the tiling level" description in Figure 3.

The kernel understands the per-channel grouping layout used for the key cache (groups formed along the channel dimension with group size G, one scale and one zero-point per (token, channel-group) tile) and indexes scales/zero-points accordingly.
The Q_MatMul kernel is numerically correct.

A unit test invokes the CUDA Q_MatMul kernel on random `q`, packed-`K`, `scale`, and `zero_point` inputs and asserts that its FP16 output matches a reference `q @ dequantize(K_packed, scale, zero_point).T` implementation within a small numerical tolerance (e.g. rel/abs error < 1e-2 for 2-bit, tighter for 4-bit).

A Triton group-wise quantization kernel is implemented that performs asymmetric B-bit round-to-nearest quantization along either the token or channel dimension with a configurable group size G, matching the description in Section 3.3.
Triton kernel and Python wrapper exist.
Code has been implemented containing a `@triton.jit`-decorated kernel that performs group-wise asymmetric quantization, packs the low-bit codes, and writes per-group scale and zero-point outputs.

Code has been implemented providing a Python wrapper that computes the Triton launch grid from tensor shape and group size G and invokes the quantization kernel with appropriate block sizes for both prefill (bulk) and decoding (single/short token dim) inputs.
The Triton kernel exposes the grouping behavior required by KIVI.
The Triton quantization kernel supports per-token grouping (used for the value cache: groups formed along the channel dimension, one (scale, zero-point) per token-group).
The Triton quantization kernel supports per-channel grouping (used for the grouped key cache X_Kg: groups formed along the token dimension, one (scale, zero-point) per channel per token-group).
The group size G is a runtime/constexpr kernel argument (not hard-coded), and the kernel is exercised at G ∈ {32, 64, 128} as required by the group-size ablation.

The Triton kernel emits asymmetric quantization outputs consistent with Section 3.1: `zX = min(X)` and `sX = (max(X) - min(X)) / (2^B - 1)` computed per group, and the quantized codes are stored as unsigned B-bit integers (B ∈ {2, 4}) in a packed buffer.
The Triton kernel is numerically correct.

A unit test runs the Triton quantization kernel on random tensors at B ∈ {2, 4} and G = 32, then dequantizes the packed output and asserts that the resulting tensor matches a pure-PyTorch reference `quantize(X)`/`dequantize(...)` implementation of the same asymmetric RTN formula bit-for-bit (or within floating-point rounding).
The Q_MatMul CUDA kernel and Triton quantization kernel are wired into the transformer attention forward path so that KIVI's prefill/decoding runs end-to-end use them.

Code has been implemented that monkey-patches or subclasses the HuggingFace Transformers attention module for Llama/Llama-2, Mistral, and Falcon so that the modified attention forward calls the KIVI kernels instead of the stock FP16 attention.

During decoding, the modified attention path invokes the fused CUDA Q_MatMul kernel to compute `t_Q @ Q(X_Kg)^T` on the grouped/quantized portion of the key cache (rather than dequantizing to FP16 and calling `torch.matmul`).

The residual key cache X_Kr (kept in full precision) is multiplied against the query using a standard FP16 matmul, and its logits are concatenated with the Q_MatMul output along the token dimension to form the raw attention logits (matching the tiled-matmul expression in Section 3.3).

The attention output is computed as `A_g @ Q(X_Vg) + A_r @ X_Vr` (per Algorithm 1), using the fused-dequant kernel path for the grouped/quantized value portion and a standard FP16 matmul for the residual value portion.

During the prefill phase, the modified attention returns the full-precision X_K and X_V to the next layer (as stated in Section 3.3) while asynchronously invoking the Triton quantization kernel to populate Q(X_Kg), X_Kr, Q(X_Vg), X_Vr into the KV cache.

The kernel integration does not touch model weight layouts, so KIVI's attention path remains compatible with weight-only quantization schemes (e.g. AWQ/GPTQ INT4 weights) as claimed at the end of Section 3.3.

Kernel-level efficiency of the fused CUDA and Triton implementations is validated so that the KIVI attention path does not regress against the FP16 baseline and delivers the fused-dequant speed advantage described in Section 3.3.

A microbenchmark measures the wall-clock latency of the fused CUDA Q_MatMul kernel at decode-relevant shapes (batch ≥ 1, single query row, key length in the low-thousands) and shows it is faster than a naive `dequantize(K) then torch.matmul` reference at the same shape/precision.

An end-to-end kernel-path sanity benchmark on Llama-2-7B decoding on a single A100 (80GB), using the ShareGPT-style workload with prompt length ~161 and generation length ~338, confirms that KIVI's kernel path does not decrease per-token decode throughput relative to the FP16 baseline at matched batch size (necessary condition for the 2.35×–3.47× throughput gains reported for KIVI).
